activities.anchor: Bias, privacy erosion, opacity and consent gaps
activities.caption: pair each failure with its working fix
activities.name: ethFixMatch

config.prompt: Each panel pairs a failure with a fix that carries a visible cost — pair them:

pairs.right: a documented policy choice, not a technical default
calibrated noise with an explicit budget
design effort for consent that means something

config.why: Each fix carries a visible cost — accuracy traded for protection, design effort traded for meaning — and tracking where the cost lands is the professional habit.

activities.caption: true or false — the audit's timing
activities.name: ethAuditJudge

config.statement: The ethical audit of a model can safely wait until after deployment, since any harms can be corrected later by retraining.
config.why: The asymmetry runs one way: a thousand users can be harmed in the minute a model is live, and none of them can see the model that did it — the audit runs before deployment.

activities.anchor: a false-positive rate of about 45% versus 23%
activities.caption: call the disparity's size
activities.name: ethCompasEst

config.prompt: COMPAS flagged Black defendants who did not reoffend high-risk about 45% of the time, versus about 23% for white non-reoffenders. Roughly how many times higher is the Black rate?
config.why: Nearly twice — and the vendor's rebuttal was also true: the score was calibrated, a 7 meaning the same recidivism probability for both groups. Both things held simultaneously.
config.context: ProPublica's 2016 analysis of roughly 7,000 Broward County defendants

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the engine that taught itself bias
activities.name: ethAmazonCloze

config.text: Amazon's experimental recruiting engine was trained on ten years of predominantly %%0%% hires, learned to downgrade CVs containing the word %%1%%, was never deployed — and its %%2%% of harm was the point: a biased human reviewer tires; a biased model reviews millions.
config.hint: Who did the hiring, what word got downgraded, and what made the harm fast.

activities.anchor: just remove race and gender from the inputs
activities.caption: the deletion fallacy
activities.name: ethProxyBranch

config.root: You delete race and gender from the model's inputs. Is it now unable to discriminate?

choices.label: Yes — the inputs no longer mention them
choices.feedback: Proxies reconstruct what you delete: postcode predicts race in segregated cities, shopping patterns predict pregnancy (Target's famous case), name predicts gender.

choices.label: No — measure error rates per group and audit the proxy set
choices.feedback: Deletion is not a fix; measurement is — treat the model's decisions, not its inputs, as the object of scrutiny.

choices.label: Depends on how accurate the model is
choices.feedback: Accuracy says nothing about whom it is accurate for — the decisions, not the inputs, are the object of scrutiny.

proxies.text: The model can discriminate perfectly well through features it never saw named.

measure.text: Evaluate error rates per group, audit the proxy set, and scrutinise decisions — that is the field's requirement.

acc.text: A highly accurate model can be precisely and unevenly wrong.

config.why: Deletion is not a fix; measurement is — the misconception mistakes the inputs for the object of scrutiny.

activities.caption: pair each fairness criterion with what it equalises
activities.name: ethMetricMatch

config.prompt: Pair each fairness criterion with the quantity it holds equal:

pairs.right: the same fraction of each group is selected
the same false-positive and false-negative rates in each group
a score of 7 means the same risk for everyone

config.why: Kleinberg–Mullainathan–Raghavan (2016) and Chouldechova (2017) proved calibration and equalised odds are mathematically incompatible when base rates differ — you cannot have both.

activities.anchor: A bail-setting system might reasonably prefer
activities.caption: two systems, two metrics — drag the divider
activities.name: ethPolicyCompare

config.prompt: Two systems choosing a fairness metric — drag the divider:

before.label: bail-setting
before.text: prefer equal false-positive rates — liberty wrongly denied is the error that matters

after.label: marketing
after.text: might accept parity of selection — the errors are cheaper and the base rates differ

config.why: Choosing a fairness metric is a policy decision about which errors matter, made with stakeholders and documented — what the field forbids is not any particular choice, it is the unexamined choice.

config.prompt: Sweeney showed roughly what share of the US population is unique on just three fields — ZIP code, date of birth, sex?
config.why: About 87% — which is how she re-identified the Governor of Massachusetts's medical record from a 'de-identified' state employee dataset.
config.context: combinations of innocuous fields that are jointly unique are quasi-identifiers

activities.anchor: instead of trying to scrub identifiers
activities.caption: rebuild the privacy-budget loop
activities.name: ethBudgetOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild differential privacy's mechanism — what comes first:
items: Pick the budget — smaller epsilon means more noise and stronger protection
Add calibrated noise so any one person's inclusion is statistically almost invisible
Compose many queries, spending the budget down
Re-derive the accuracy–protection trade for each use case
config.why: Privacy becomes an explicit, budgetable resource rather than a hope — with units, budgets and proofs, deployed by Apple, Google and the 2020 US Census.

activities.anchor: adding noise makes the data useless
activities.caption: find the backwards claim — the noise trade
activities.name: ethNoiseSpot

config.prompt: One of these claims about differential privacy is backwards — click it:
lines: Noise makes the data bounded, not useless.
Aggregate questions retain excellent accuracy under the budget.
Individual-level questions lose meaning — usually exactly the right trade.
The census stopped redistricting because the noise made it impossible.
config.correction: The census still redistricts; hospitals still publish; Apple still ships keyboards.
config.why: What dies is the fantasy of free, perfect, person-level data — the aggregates survive with measurable, budgeted noise.
